title: Thermostat samplekit — quickstart & playflow (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a working quickstart + interactive playflow for the "Thermostat" samplekit — a compact, opinionated example app that demonstrates common SDK integration patterns for device/web clients, streaming generation, local-sim mode, error handling, and a minimal telemetry contract. The goal is a 10–20 minute hands-on path that an engineer can follow during a workshop or as a first-run demo.

Audience:
- SDK adopters evaluating integration patterns
- Solutions engineers running workshops
- Docs/DevX writers extracting snippets and checklists

High-level goals: 
1) Show local dev loop (simulate device) + plug into hosted API quickly.
2) Demonstrate streaming response handling and UI fallback for poor networks.
3) Surface SDK error semantics (retries, idempotency keys, local caching).
4) Provide a minimal telemetry map for events to emit.
5) Offer smoke-test checklist for CI and demo reliability.

Quickstart TL;DR (10–15 min)
1) Clone example: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/sdk-examples.git && cd sdk-examples/thermostat-samplekit
2) Install: npm ci (or pip install -r requirements.txt for python variant)
3) Start simulator: npm run start-sim  # opens a tiny web UI emulating a thermostat
4) Set REDWOOD_API_KEY locally (export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_dev_xxx)
5) Run client: npm run start-client  # client uses SDK to call /generate and streams updates
6) Try toggles: change temp setpoint, ask natural-language requests ("Make it cozy for 6pm")

Playflow — sections and checkpoints
A. Local-sim mode (5 min)
- What it does: runs a tiny device simulator (node) that emits temperature/time/occupancy every 10s and accepts control messages.
- Checkpoint: simulator emits events in JSON, client prints to console.
- Notes to self: allow a --fast-forward flag for demo (1s tick) so we can show drift quickly.

B. First SDK call (3 min)
- Pattern: one-shot completion to produce a human-friendly schedule from device state.
- Code snippet (JS):
  const res = await Redwood.generate({ model: 'rwd-small-1', prompt: template(state) });
  // display res.text in UI
- Checkpoint: UI shows scheduling suggestion
- Failure mode: 401 -> prompt user to set REDWOOD_API_KEY. Add clear error banner.

C. Streaming updates (3–5 min)
- Pattern: open stream to render partial text and update a preview box.
- UX rule: show progressive text, but also show an optimistic control state if LLM signals intent early (first 30–40% tokens).
- Checkpoint: partial tokens render, stream 'done' event updates telemetry
- Failure mode: stream drop mid-response -> fallback to short completion with strict temperature/length to provide a minimal fallback message.

D. Idempotent control actions (3 min)
- Problem: network flakiness can cause duplicate device commands.
- Solution: send an idempotency_key with critical mutate requests (e.g., set-temperature). SDK helper: sdk.mutate({ action, idempotencyKey })
- Checkpoint: simulator receives only one command after simulated flaky network (use --drop-requests=1 flag)

E. Offline-first local cache (optional)
- Pattern: maintain local optimistic state and a small action-queue persisted to localStorage. On reconnect flush queue with idempotency keys.
- Checkpoint: toggle network off in client, issue command, refresh reconnect -> command applied once.

Minimal telemetry contract (what to emit)
- event: sdk.request.start — { route, model, request_type }
- event: sdk.request.stream_token — emitted periodically with token_count
- event: sdk.request.done — { latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, success true/false }
- event: samplekit.user_action — { control, idempotency_key, result }
- event: samplekit.fallback_used — { reason }
Notes: keep payloads small, don't send user PII. Add anonymized hash for request templates.

Smoke tests for CI (short list)
- unit: generate function returns non-empty string given sample state (fast)
- integration: start simulator bind to port, run client e2e script, assert it receives at least 3 telemetry events
- resilience: run client with --drop-requests=2 and assert idempotent behavior
- latency guard (optional): assert average token latency < 250ms in CI environment (mocked)

UX anti-patterns to avoid
- Blocking UI on completion: always render partials and provide cancel button.
- Showing raw LLM JSON to users. Transform into intent+action.
- Blind auto-apply commands without a confirmation affordance when opinionated (i.e., when action is not trivially reversible).

Developer notes / TODOs
- Add Python variant of quickstart (currently JS-only).
- Create a one-page detachable cheat-sheet for solutions engineers (commands, env vars, quick checks).
- Record a 4–5 minute demo video for docs landing page.
- Consider adding a local pre-seeded prompt-set for reproducible outputs across runs (seed param in run-sim).

Open questions (for product/dev lead)
- Which model tags should be recommended for tight-latency demos? rwd-small-1 vs rwd-medium-1? Need guidance from runtime team.
- What is the official telemetry destination URL and retention policy for demo telemetry? (security/compliance check)

Appendix: quick check commands
- Start sim: npm run start-sim -- --port=3100
- Run client dev: npm run start-client -- --ui=chromium
- Simulate flaky network: node tools/dropper.js --target=client --count=1
- Reset telemetry database (local): ./scripts/reset-telemetry.sh

Notes-to-self: keep the text conversational and short; this doc will seed a separate polished quickstart on the docs site. During the next workshop iteration, gather where devs get stuck (auth, streaming, idempotency) and fold into the cheat-sheet.

End of draft.
